top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B040) has the cleanest attribution on the slate: a two-author originating paper with no co-originator left out, and nearly three decades of extension, criticism and use in macro-finance and crisis modelling. The citation should claim the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles are modelled, not a settled magnitude of amplification. I treat the thin direct empirical validation as the main reservation, and the Committee should say openly that excluding Gertler and Gilchrist favours theory over tested evidence. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, narrowed to trade-shock evidence) is a close second. It is credibly identified and replicated, but it is about a decade younger, and the debates over shift-share inference and the size and persistence of the effects are unresolved. P003 (BLP demand estimation) is mature and influential, but it is a methods contribution whose credibility depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions, and its credit boundary with the wider structural-IO programme is less clean. P000 is ranked last because at least three candidates are substantive, mature and attributable.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. My metascience orientation may make me more receptive to replicated empirical designs, and I applied the common criteria regardless.
